title: Are Central Banks Moving Out of Dollar Assets? - Liberty Street Economics
gist: The dollar's share of global official FX reserves fell from 64 percent in 2015 to 56 percent in 2025, but a country-level decomposition into a "preferences channel" (active reallocation) and a "reserve change channel" (mechanical reweighting) shows the drop is not broad-based de-dollarization. Roughly equal numbers of countries raised and cut dollar shares over each four-year window; the aggregate decline is concentrated in China and Russia (plus Switzerland's mechanical drag in 2015-19), and for 2019-23 an implied -2.0 percentage points comes from just four non-disclosing holders: China, Russia, Mexico, and Morocco.

insights.claim: New York Fed research argues the decade-long decline in the dollar's aggregate reserve share is not a systematic global shift out of dollar assets but the arithmetic result of a handful of large reserve holders changing either currency preferences or portfolio size.

insights.so_what: Undercuts the core macro thesis behind structural short-dollar and reserve-diversification trades; the aggregate is a weighted average, not a vote count.

insights.claim: The pace of decline in the dollar's reserve share slowed between periods: it fell 3 percentage points from 2015 to 2019 and 2 percentage points from 2019 to 2023, with the underlying IMF COFER moves put at 2.8 and 2.3 percentage points respectively.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Deceleration in the post-2019 window argues against an accelerating de-dollarization narrative tied to sanctions-era headlines.

insights.claim: Across both four-year windows examined, roughly equal numbers of countries increased and decreased their dollar reserve share, with countries moving less than 0.5 percentage point classified as no change.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: A simple directional count is the cheapest falsification test for the de-dollarization thesis, and it fails to support it.

insights.claim: A decomposition framework splits changes in the global dollar reserve share into a "preferences channel" — countries actively reallocating existing portfolios between currencies — and a "reserve change channel" — countries accumulating or running down reserves at dollar shares different from the global average.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Gives a reusable lens for reading any future COFER print: ask whether the move came from intent or from balance-sheet size.
insights.locator: Understanding the Aggregate Dollar Shares of Reserves

insights.claim: When a country whose dollar allocation is below the global average expands its reserve stock, the size-weighted global dollar share falls mechanically even though that country has not reduced its own dollar allocation at all.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Explains how a falling headline dollar share can coexist with rising or flat dollar demand — the reserve-share statistic is not a demand proxy.
insights.quote: When a country with below-average dollar holdings expands its reserves, it mechanically pulls down the global aggregate, even without reducing its own allocation to dollars.
insights.locator: Understanding the Aggregate Dollar Shares of Reserves

insights.claim: For the 2015-19 window, seventy-nine country reserve portfolios were examined and seventy-six had complete start- and end-period data, with the decline split almost evenly between the preferences channel at 1.2 percentage points and the reserve change channel at 1.5 percentage points.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Roughly half the mid-2010s dollar-share decline was mechanical, not a portfolio decision — halving the size of any genuine diversification signal.

insights.claim: A single reserve holder can push the global dollar share in opposite directions through the two channels at once, so channel-level netting hides offsetting forces that an aggregate number presents as a uniform trend.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Warns against inferring any country's dollar intent from its net contribution to the headline; intent lives only in the preferences channel.

insights.claim: Because larger reserve holders exert disproportionate influence on the size-weighted global dollar share, the headline statistic can mask two fundamentally different phenomena — deliberate currency reallocation and pure portfolio-size effects.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Any macro model keying off COFER should decompose it first; the raw series conflates intent with scale.

themes.theme: 2015-19: China, Russia and the Swiss Paradox

insights.claim: China and Russia dominated the preferences channel over 2015-19, accounting for most of the 1.2 percentage point global decline attributable to active reallocation away from dollar assets.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Genuine official de-dollarization is a two-country geopolitical story, not a global one — trade it as sanctions/geopolitical risk, not as a secular dollar theme.
insights.locator: The preferences channel captures active reallocation

insights.claim: Outside China and Russia, active reallocation away from the dollar over 2015-19 was tiny — Turkey, Peru, and Spain each contributed only around negative 0.2 percentage point — while Sweden and Switzerland actually raised their dollar portfolio shares.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Shows the second tier of the de-dollarization story is an order of magnitude smaller and partly offset by developed-market dollar buying.
insights.locator: The preferences channel captures active reallocation

insights.claim: Switzerland was the largest single negative contributor to the global dollar reserve share via the reserve change channel over 2015-19 purely because its below-average dollar share combined with large-scale reserve accumulation, even while it was simultaneously raising its own dollar allocation.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: The cleanest illustration that the headline dollar-share drop can be driven by a country that is buying more dollars, not fewer.

insights.claim: The Czech Republic and Russia also dragged the global dollar share down mechanically over 2015-19 by accumulating reserves at below-average dollar shares, while Hong Kong and China contributed positively through that channel — China's positive contribution coming from reserve drawdowns.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: China simultaneously cut dollar preference and propped up the global dollar share by shrinking reserves — a case study in why net numbers mislead.

insights.claim: Several of the largest reserve holders that reported currency composition in 2019 stopped disclosing their 2023 dollar allocations, with China, Russia, Mexico, and Morocco the biggest among the non-disclosers, leaving complete data for only sixty-two countries.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: The most consequential reserve managers have gone dark on currency composition — treat any post-2019 attribution of dollar-share moves as inference, not observation.

insights.claim: China, Russia, Mexico, and Morocco together hold reserves roughly equal in size to the entire remaining sixty-two-country sample combined, making their non-disclosure decisive for any global currency-composition estimate.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Half the observable universe of reserves is now unobservable by currency — a structural data risk for anyone modelling official dollar demand.

insights.so_what: The transparent majority of reserve managers were net dollar buyers by preference in 2019-23, the opposite of the headline narrative.

themes.theme: What Actually Drives Official Dollar Demand

insights.claim: Official reserve holdings are driven by country needs for dollar liquidity, currency management needs, and insurance against funding shocks, and those structural drivers are judged to still retain their strength.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: The functional demand base for dollar reserves is intact, so any diversification must overcome liquidity and insurance needs, not just political preference.
insights.quote: Official reserve holdings traditionally are driven by country needs for dollar liquidity, currency management needs, and insurance against both funding shocks.

insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate the current mechanical drag forward — its contributors are not persistent and carry no directional dollar view.

insights.claim: For policymakers and market participants, the decomposition indicates there is little evidence of a widespread official diversification away from dollars despite the visible decline in the aggregate official dollar share.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: An explicit central-bank-research pushback against the reserve-diversification narrative; a fade signal for trades premised on broad official dollar exit.

insights.claim: Aggregate reserve statistics can create misleading impressions of broad trends when they in fact reflect the concentrated actions of a few large players, so interpreting the dollar's international role requires country-level concentration analysis.
insights.speaker: John Lanuza
insights.so_what: Generalizable method: before trading a macro aggregate, check whether its move is broad-based or driven by two or three balance sheets.
